title: Global Semiconductor Equipment Giants: Competitive Landscape & Innovations in Advanced Packaging Technology - 36Kr
query: "Applied Materials" ("hybrid bonding" OR "wafer bonding" OR "advanced packaging" OR "bonding equipment" OR "die bonding" OR "semiconductor packaging") after:2026-10-01 before:2026-11-01
discovery_snippet: Global Semiconductor Equipment Giants: Competitive Landscape & Innovations in Advanced Packaging Technology    36Kr
content_text:
Equipment giants are vying for advanced packaging
半导体行业观察 2026-10-19 10:59 
Today, the competition among equipment vendors centering on hybrid bonding is essentially an early strategic layout for the dominance of the future 3D integrated manufacturing process. 
In early October, a piece of news in the capital market drew widespread attention: over concerns that ASML may enter the hybrid bonding equipment market and the demand for HBM-related equipment will be postponed, Bank of America downgraded the investment rating of Besi, a Dutch packaging equipment manufacturer, on October 6, driving its share price down 5.39% on the same day; the next day, as UBS further downgraded its rating, Besi's share price fell another 8.49%, with a cumulative drop of about 13.4% in just two trading days. In fact, ASML delivered the TWINSCAN XT:260 lithography system for advanced packaging as early as 2025, and news of its R&D of hybrid bonding equipment came out this year, further expanding its business beyond traditional lithography.
Overview of Besi's stock price trend (Source: Yahoo)
Meanwhile, Applied Materials and Lam Research are also accelerating their layout. In the first week of October alone, Applied Materials successively announced deepened cooperation with Besi and Intel, with R&D scope covering hybrid bonding, TCB, chip-to-panel, Foveros 3D packaging and other technologies. Leveraging technologies such as etching, deposition and copper electroplating, Lam Research continues to expand its equipment layout in the fields of TSV and 3D interconnection. In March this year, Reuters reported that both Lam Research and Applied Materials showed acquisition interest in Besi.
It can be seen that the three giants of front-end equipment are extending to advanced packaging along different technical routes. On the one hand, the front-end equipment giants are actively extending to advanced packaging, and on the other hand, the traditional leading packaging equipment manufacturers have become the targets of cooperation, investment and even potential mergers and acquisitions. The originally relatively clear division of labor between front-end and back-end in the semiconductor equipment industry is undergoing subtle changes. Advanced packaging is becoming a new battlefield that semiconductor equipment giants are vying to enter. 
The Three Front-End Equipment Giants Are Surrounding Advanced Packaging 
In fact, a closer look shows that although Applied Materials, Lam Research and ASML are all extending to the advanced packaging field, the three have chosen different entry methods.
Applied Materials pays more attention to material engineering and process integration, and builds comprehensive solutions covering multiple manufacturing links by cooperating with professional packaging equipment manufacturers; Lam Research relies on etching, deposition and copper interconnection technologies to compete for more and more key process steps in the 3D integration process; ASML has begun to try to extend its accumulated nanoscale motion control, precision alignment and measurement technologies in the lithography field to hybrid bonding equipment.
These three routes are complementary to each other, and may gradually form direct competition as technology evolves.
Applied Materials: Join hands with Besi to build a complete process chain
First of all, talking about Applied Materials, its layout in advanced packaging has actually lasted for many years.
As early as 2020, Applied Materials and Besi established a joint R&D project in Singapore, combining its own technologies in etching, planarization, thin film deposition, wafer cleaning, metrology and inspection, and particle control with Besi's capabilities in precision chip mounting, interconnection and assembly.
The representative achievement of the cooperation between the two parties is the Kinex integrated Die-to-Wafer (D2W) hybrid bonding system. Different from traditional packaging equipment that mainly focuses on chip mounting and connection, Kinex attempts to integrate pre-bonding processes such as surface treatment, cleaning, activation and alignment into a more compact manufacturing flow.
Kinex (Image source: Applied Materials)
This design has practical significance.
In the hybrid bonding process, the two chips or wafers to be connected must not only achieve extremely high-precision geometric alignment, but also ensure the flatness, cleanliness and material state of the bonding surface. Even if the bonding equipment itself has excellent positioning accuracy, if the previous process causes particle pollution, abnormal copper pad depression or unstable surface state, it may still lead to connection defects. The cooperation between Applied Materials and Besi is essentially an attempt to combine traditional front-end material engineering with back-end precision assembly technology to improve the final yield through cross-process collaboration.
It is worth noting that Applied Materials does not limit technical cooperation to Besi alone. Previously, it also cooperated with EV Group (EVG), an Austrian wafer bonding equipment manufacturer, to develop wafer-to-wafer bonding solutions.
The cooperation upgrade on October 1 this year further expanded the R&D boundary of both parties. According to the official announcement, Besi will become an innovation partner of Applied Materials' EPIC R&D center located in Silicon Valley. In the future, the two parties will not only continue to promote D2W hybrid bonding, but also jointly research TCB process scaling, chip-to-chip, chip-to-panel and new integration architectures for optical interconnection. The EPIC center is planned to have a maximum investment scale of about 5 billion US dollars, and the investment will be gradually rolled out as customer projects advance. An important goal of this center is to enable chip manufacturers, equipment suppliers and material enterprises to participate in joint R&D at an earlier stage, shortening the cycle for new processes to move from the laboratory to mass production.
From the perspective of industrial significance, this means that Applied Materials is trying to incorporate advanced packaging, which was previously a relatively independent back-end manufacturing link, into its broader material engineering R&D system.
Just five days later, Applied Materials announced the deepening of cooperation with Intel, covering R&D of next-generation transistors, on-chip interconnection and Foveros 3D advanced packaging.
These two cooperations seem to target different enterprises, but their technical logic is connected. In 3D stacking, there are complex interactions between interconnection density, power supply paths, heat dissipation structures and material stress between chips. The performance optimization of next-generation chips is increasingly difficult to achieve by relying solely on one link among advanced process, metal interconnection or packaging.
Therefore, for Applied Materials, the real strategic value may not only be to obtain more orders for hybrid bonding equipment, but to participate in the definition of next-generation chip manufacturing processes earlier through the joint development of front-end and back-end processes. As Prabu Raja from Applied Materials asserted: Advanced packaging is no longer just the physical assembly of the back-end, but a material engineering revolution that requires wafer-level precision and cleanliness.
Lam Research: From Etching, Deposition to 3D Interconnection 
Compared with the cooperation model between Applied Materials and Besi, Lam Research's layout in the advanced packaging field highlights its existing process and equipment advantages. Lam Research has accumulated a large number of high-aspect-ratio etching, thin film deposition and metal interconnection technologies in the past in the manufacture of logic chips, DRAM and 3D NAND.
With the continuous 3D development of advanced packaging, these technologies are gaining more application scenarios. For example, in 3D stacked chips, Through-Silicon Vias (TSVs) undertake vertical electrical connections between different chip layers. To make deep and narrow vias in silicon wafers, high-aspect-ratio etching technology is required, and the via sidewall morphology, etching uniformity and defect control should be guaranteed as much as possible.
Lam Research's Syndion deep reactive ion etching equipment is designed for deep hole etching requirements including TSV. But etching the via is only the first step. After forming the insulating layer, barrier layer and seed layer, the via needs to be filled by metal deposition to form a reliable electrical connection. If voids, seams or other defects occur during the copper filling process, it may affect resistance, heat dissipation and long-term reliability.
The SABRE 3D copper electroplating platform that Lam Research highlighted in July this year is developed around the manufacturing needs of complex metal interconnection in advanced packaging. The company emphasizes that as the interconnection structure of advanced packaging becomes more and more refined, the requirements for metal filling uniformity and void control in the manufacturing process are continuously increasing. SABRE 3D provides metal filling capabilities for structures such as TSV, wafer-level packaging and redistribution layers through electrochemical deposition processes.
In addition, Lam Research has also deployed the VECTOR TEOS 3D dielectric material deposition equipment, as well as related wet and deposition processes for large-sized substrates.
It is worth noting that the attraction of advanced packaging to Lam Research is not just hybrid bonding itself. From traditional 2.5D packaging to 3D chip stacking, and then to panel-level packaging, more and more manufacturing steps require high-precision etching, thin film deposition and metal interconnection processes, which are the fields that Lam Research has long been deeply engaged in.
Therefore, Lam Research's competitive logic is not necessarily to directly replace Besi to manufacture bonding equipment, but to obtain more value in the advanced packaging industry chain by expanding the coverage of key process equipment.
However, the company's interest in bonding equipment is also worthy of attention. In March 2026, Reuters, citing people familiar with the matter, reported that Besi has attracted the attention of potential acquirers due to its hybrid bonding technology, and both Lam Research and Applied Materials are on the relevant list.
For Lam Research, if it wants to further expand into direct bonding equipment, leveraging professional equipment enterprises that already have a customer base and mass production experience may help it establish market position faster than relying entirely on internal R&D.
However, up to now, public reports have not confirmed that the relevant acquisition transaction has finally been reached. This also reveals some information: the next round of competition in the advanced packaging equipment industry may be accompanied by equity investment, strategic cooperation and even industrial integration in addition to technology R&D and product upgrading.
ASML: From Lithography to Hybrid Bonding, Directly Challenging Besi? 
It can be seen that the advanced packaging business of Applied Materials and Lam Research mainly stems from the horizontal extension of their existing material engineering capabilities. However, ASML's potential entry may have a more direct impact on the traditional hybrid bonding equipment market.
As the exclusive global supplier of EUV lithography equipment, ASML's core technical accumulation is concentrated in the fields of high-precision optics, motion control, wafer positioning, deformation compensation and nanoscale overlay accuracy.
In the past, these technologies were mainly used to accurately transfer increasingly tiny circuit patterns to the wafer surface. However, in hybrid bonding, there is also a very critical problem to be solved: how to accurately align the metal interconnection structures on two wafers or different chips and maintain stability during the bonding process. Therefore, there is a certain degree of commonality between ASML's original technical capabilities and hybrid bonding equipment. 
In fact, ASML has already entered the advanced packaging market through dedicated lithography equipment. At the annual general meeting of shareholders held in April 2026, ASML disclosed that the company has delivered the first TWINSCAN XT:260 i-line lithography system, which is specially designed for 3D integration and advanced packaging applications. Different from EUV scanners, which are mainly used for advanced logic processes, the XT:260 targets special patterning requirements in advanced packaging. ASML pointed out in its demonstration materials that the micro-bump process requires a large depth of focus, while hybrid bonding puts forward higher requirements for pattern resolution. This means that as the interconnection density of advanced packaging continues to increase, lithography itself has begun to become an important link affecting the evolution of packaging technology.
The TWINSCAN XT:260 launched by ASML last year is an i-line scanner that can process 270 wafers per hour. In view of the growing demand for AI chips, ASML plans to shift its business focus from pure front-end chip production equipment to packaging and bonding technologies in the next 10 to 15 years. (Image source: ASML)
But ASML is obviously not satisfied with only providing advanced packaging lithography equipment.
In March this year, South Korean media The Elec reported that ASML has started the overall architecture design of hybrid bonding equipment and has been in contact for cooperation with long-term suppliers such as Prodrive Technologies and VDL ETG. These enterprises previously participated in the supply of precision motion systems, drive devices and mechanical structures for ASML's lithography equipment. If ASML tries to transfer its accumulation in high-precision motion platforms to bonding equipment, it may further narrow the technical distance between lithography equipment and hybrid bonding equipment.
Moreover, there is another point worthy of attention that ASML has already published related patents.
The international patent WO2026098870A1 published on May 15, 2026 is titled "Bonding Apparatus", with the applicant being ASML Netherlands BV. The patent relates to a bonding device for two semiconductor substrates, focusing on discussing how to improve the alignment problem that may occur in the bonding process through state control of the substrate support surface. The patent document points out that factors such as internal stress of the wafer, support surface state and flatness may cause alignment deviation during bonding. This is obviously related to ASML's long-term research on wafer deformation compensation, position measurement and precision motion control technologies.
Of course, patent layout does not mean that mass-produced equipment is already mature. ASML has not yet publicly confirmed the commercial delivery time, customer certification progress or mass production performance of its hybrid bonding equipment. But this potential competition has begun to affect the market's expectations for traditional equipment enterprises. On October 6, Bank of America downgraded Besi's investment rating, which mentioned the competitive risk that ASML may enter the hybrid bonding market in the future.
For Besi, this risk is worthy of attention. In the traditional advanced packaging equipment market, Besi's important advantages come from long-term accumulation in precision mounting, assembly processes and hybrid bonding technology. Once ASML officially enters, it may form a new competitive force with its experience in nanoscale positioning, precision measurement and large-scale complex equipment system engineering.
However, from having key technical capabilities to developing competitive commercial equipment and then passing the mass production certification of wafer fabs, there is still a considerable long process of technology and commercialization.
Whether ASML can really challenge Besi ultimately depends on the alignment accuracy, throughput, yield, equipment stability, cost and customer certification progress of the equipment, and cannot be judged solely based on patents or supply chain news.
Why Has Hybrid Bonding Become the Focus of Competition? 
An important background for front-end equipment giants to enter advanced packaging one after another is that chip interconnection technology is changing.
In traditional 2.5D and 3D packaging, chips usually establish electrical connections through Micro-bumps. Thermal Compression Bonding (TCB) achieves reliable connection between solder and metal pads by applying temperature and pressure. This process is widely used in the field of high-performance computing and memory chips, but with the increase of chip stacking layers and the improvement of interconnection density, traditional micro-bump structures are gradually facing higher requirements in terms of pitch, connection height, parasitic effect and thermomechanical reliability.
Hybrid bonding provides another technical route. It combines direct dielectric bonding with metal interconnection to reduce the dependence on traditional solder bumps, thus making it possible to achieve smaller interconnection pitch, higher connection density and more compact chip stacking structure.
In May 2026, Imec, the Belgian microelectronics research center, and EV Group announced that they had achieved a 200nm copper interconnection pitch in wafer-to-wafer hybrid bonding research. The research team achieved a post-bond copper pad overlay deviation of less than 40nm for all test chips on 300mm wafers.
Transmission electron microscope image of the daisy chain structure on a 200nm hexagonal pad grid with hybrid pads of the same size and 25% designed copper density. (Image source: imec/IEEE)

content_text:
Equipment giants are vying for advanced packaging
半导体行业观察 2026-10-19 10:59 
Today, the competition among equipment vendors centering on hybrid bonding is essentially an early strategic layout for the dominance of the future 3D integrated manufacturing process. 
In early October, a piece of news in the capital market drew widespread attention: over concerns that ASML may enter the hybrid bonding equipment market and the demand for HBM-related equipment will be postponed, Bank of America downgraded the investment rating of Besi, a Dutch packaging equipment manufacturer, on October 6, driving its share price down 5.39% on the same day; the next day, as UBS further downgraded its rating, Besi's share price fell another 8.49%, with a cumulative drop of about 13.4% in just two trading days. In fact, ASML delivered the TWINSCAN XT:260 lithography system for advanced packaging as early as 2025, and news of its R&D of hybrid bonding equipment came out this year, further expanding its business beyond traditional lithography.
Overview of Besi's stock price trend (Source: Yahoo)
Meanwhile, Applied Materials and Lam Research are also accelerating their layout. In the first week of October alone, Applied Materials successively announced deepened cooperation with Besi and Intel, with R&D scope covering hybrid bonding, TCB, chip-to-panel, Foveros 3D packaging and other technologies. Leveraging technologies such as etching, deposition and copper electroplating, Lam Research continues to expand its equipment layout in the fields of TSV and 3D interconnection. In March this year, Reuters reported that both Lam Research and Applied Materials showed acquisition interest in Besi.
It can be seen that the three giants of front-end equipment are extending to advanced packaging along different technical routes. On the one hand, the front-end equipment giants are actively extending to advanced packaging, and on the other hand, the traditional leading packaging equipment manufacturers have become the targets of cooperation, investment and even potential mergers and acquisitions. The originally relatively clear division of labor between front-end and back-end in the semiconductor equipment industry is undergoing subtle changes. Advanced packaging is becoming a new battlefield that semiconductor equipment giants are vying to enter. 
The Three Front-End Equipment Giants Are Surrounding Advanced Packaging 
In fact, a closer look shows that although Applied Materials, Lam Research and ASML are all extending to the advanced packaging field, the three have chosen different entry methods.
Applied Materials pays more attention to material engineering and process integration, and builds comprehensive solutions covering multiple manufacturing links by cooperating with professional packaging equipment manufacturers; Lam Research relies on etching, deposition and copper interconnection technologies to compete for more and more key process steps in the 3D integration process; ASML has begun to try to extend its accumulated nanoscale motion control, precision alignment and measurement technologies in the lithography field to hybrid bonding equipment.
These three routes are complementary to each other, and may gradually form direct competition as technology evolves.
Applied Materials: Join hands with Besi to build a complete process chain
First of all, talking about Applied Materials, its layout in advanced packaging has actually lasted for many years.
As early as 2020, Applied Materials and Besi established a joint R&D project in Singapore, combining its own technologies in etching, planarization, thin film deposition, wafer cleaning, metrology and inspection, and particle control with Besi's capabilities in precision chip mounting, interconnection and assembly.
The representative achievement of the cooperation between the two parties is the Kinex integrated Die-to-Wafer (D2W) hybrid bonding system. Different from traditional packaging equipment that mainly focuses on chip mounting and connection, Kinex attempts to integrate pre-bonding processes such as surface treatment, cleaning, activation and alignment into a more compact manufacturing flow.
Kinex (Image source: Applied Materials)
This design has practical significance.
In the hybrid bonding process, the two chips or wafers to be connected must not only achieve extremely high-precision geometric alignment, but also ensure the flatness, cleanliness and material state of the bonding surface. Even if the bonding equipment itself has excellent positioning accuracy, if the previous process causes particle pollution, abnormal copper pad depression or unstable surface state, it may still lead to connection defects. The cooperation between Applied Materials and Besi is essentially an attempt to combine traditional front-end material engineering with back-end precision assembly technology to improve the final yield through cross-process collaboration.
It is worth noting that Applied Materials does not limit technical cooperation to Besi alone. Previously, it also cooperated with EV Group (EVG), an Austrian wafer bonding equipment manufacturer, to develop wafer-to-wafer bonding solutions.
The cooperation upgrade on October 1 this year further expanded the R&D boundary of both parties. According to the official announcement, Besi will become an innovation partner of Applied Materials' EPIC R&D center located in Silicon Valley. In the future, the two parties will not only continue to promote D2W hybrid bonding, but also jointly research TCB process scaling, chip-to-chip, chip-to-panel and new integration architectures for optical interconnection. The EPIC center is planned to have a maximum investment scale of about 5 billion US dollars, and the investment will be gradually rolled out as customer projects advance. An important goal of this center is to enable chip manufacturers, equipment suppliers and material enterprises to participate in joint R&D at an earlier stage, shortening the cycle for new processes to move from the laboratory to mass production.
From the perspective of industrial significance, this means that Applied Materials is trying to incorporate advanced packaging, which was previously a relatively independent back-end manufacturing link, into its broader material engineering R&D system.
Just five days later, Applied Materials announced the deepening of cooperation with Intel, covering R&D of next-generation transistors, on-chip interconnection and Foveros 3D advanced packaging.
These two cooperations seem to target different enterprises, but their technical logic is connected. In 3D stacking, there are complex interactions between interconnection density, power supply paths, heat dissipation structures and material stress between chips. The performance optimization of next-generation chips is increasingly difficult to achieve by relying solely on one link among advanced process, metal interconnection or packaging.
Therefore, for Applied Materials, the real strategic value may not only be to obtain more orders for hybrid bonding equipment, but to participate in the definition of next-generation chip manufacturing processes earlier through the joint development of front-end and back-end processes. As Prabu Raja from Applied Materials asserted: Advanced packaging is no longer just the physical assembly of the back-end, but a material engineering revolution that requires wafer-level precision and cleanliness.
Lam Research: From Etching, Deposition to 3D Interconnection 
Compared with the cooperation model between Applied Materials and Besi, Lam Research's layout in the advanced packaging field highlights its existing process and equipment advantages. Lam Research has accumulated a large number of high-aspect-ratio etching, thin film deposition and metal interconnection technologies in the past in the manufacture of logic chips, DRAM and 3D NAND.
With the continuous 3D development of advanced packaging, these technologies are gaining more application scenarios. For example, in 3D stacked chips, Through-Silicon Vias (TSVs) undertake vertical electrical connections between different chip layers. To make deep and narrow vias in silicon wafers, high-aspect-ratio etching technology is required, and the via sidewall morphology, etching uniformity and defect control should be guaranteed as much as possible.
Lam Research's Syndion deep reactive ion etching equipment is designed for deep hole etching requirements including TSV. But etching the via is only the first step. After forming the insulating layer, barrier layer and seed layer, the via needs to be filled by metal deposition to form a reliable electrical connection. If voids, seams or other defects occur during the copper filling process, it may affect resistance, heat dissipation and long-term reliability.
The SABRE 3D copper electroplating platform that Lam Research highlighted in July this year is developed around the manufacturing needs of complex metal interconnection in advanced packaging. The company emphasizes that as the interconnection structure of advanced packaging becomes more and more refined, the requirements for metal filling uniformity and void control in the manufacturing process are continuously increasing. SABRE 3D provides metal filling capabilities for structures such as TSV, wafer-level packaging and redistribution layers through electrochemical deposition processes.
In addition, Lam Research has also deployed the VECTOR TEOS 3D dielectric material deposition equipment, as well as related wet and deposition processes for large-sized substrates.
It is worth noting that the attraction of advanced packaging to Lam Research is not just hybrid bonding itself. From traditional 2.5D packaging to 3D chip stacking, and then to panel-level packaging, more and more manufacturing steps require high-precision etching, thin film deposition and metal interconnection processes, which are the fields that Lam Research has long been deeply engaged in.
Therefore, Lam Research's competitive logic is not necessarily to directly replace Besi to manufacture bonding equipment, but to obtain more value in the advanced packaging industry chain by expanding the coverage of key process equipment.
However, the company's interest in bonding equipment is also worthy of attention. In March 2026, Reuters, citing people familiar with the matter, reported that Besi has attracted the attention of potential acquirers due to its hybrid bonding technology, and both Lam Research and Applied Materials are on the relevant list.
For Lam Research, if it wants to further expand into direct bonding equipment, leveraging professional equipment enterprises that already have a customer base and mass production experience may help it establish market position faster than relying entirely on internal R&D.
However, up to now, public reports have not confirmed that the relevant acquisition transaction has finally been reached. This also reveals some information: the next round of competition in the advanced packaging equipment industry may be accompanied by equity investment, strategic cooperation and even industrial integration in addition to technology R&D and product upgrading.
ASML: From Lithography to Hybrid Bonding, Directly Challenging Besi? 
It can be seen that the advanced packaging business of Applied Materials and Lam Research mainly stems from the horizontal extension of their existing material engineering capabilities. However, ASML's potential entry may have a more direct impact on the traditional hybrid bonding equipment market.
As the exclusive global supplier of EUV lithography equipment, ASML's core technical accumulation is concentrated in the fields of high-precision optics, motion control, wafer positioning, deformation compensation and nanoscale overlay accuracy.
In the past, these technologies were mainly used to accurately transfer increasingly tiny circuit patterns to the wafer surface. However, in hybrid bonding, there is also a very critical problem to be solved: how to accurately align the metal interconnection structures on two wafers or different chips and maintain stability during the bonding process. Therefore, there is a certain degree of commonality between ASML's original technical capabilities and hybrid bonding equipment. 
In fact, ASML has already entered the advanced packaging market through dedicated lithography equipment. At the annual general meeting of shareholders held in April 2026, ASML disclosed that the company has delivered the first TWINSCAN XT:260 i-line lithography system, which is specially designed for 3D integration and advanced packaging applications. Different from EUV scanners, which are mainly used for advanced logic processes, the XT:260 targets special patterning requirements in advanced packaging. ASML pointed out in its demonstration materials that the micro-bump process requires a large depth of focus, while hybrid bonding puts forward higher requirements for pattern resolution. This means that as the interconnection density of advanced packaging continues to increase, lithography itself has begun to become an important link affecting the evolution of packaging technology.
The TWINSCAN XT:260 launched by ASML last year is an i-line scanner that can process 270 wafers per hour. In view of the growing demand for AI chips, ASML plans to shift its business focus from pure front-end chip production equipment to packaging and bonding technologies in the next 10 to 15 years. (Image source: ASML)
But ASML is obviously not satisfied with only providing advanced packaging lithography equipment.
In March this year, South Korean media The Elec reported that ASML has started the overall architecture design of hybrid bonding equipment and has been in contact for cooperation with long-term suppliers such as Prodrive Technologies and VDL ETG. These enterprises previously participated in the supply of precision motion systems, drive devices and mechanical structures for ASML's lithography equipment. If ASML tries to transfer its accumulation in high-precision motion platforms to bonding equipment, it may further narrow the technical distance between lithography equipment and hybrid bonding equipment.
Moreover, there is another point worthy of attention that ASML has already published related patents.
The international patent WO2026098870A1 published on May 15, 2026 is titled "Bonding Apparatus", with the applicant being ASML Netherlands BV. The patent relates to a bonding device for two semiconductor substrates, focusing on discussing how to improve the alignment problem that may occur in the bonding process through state control of the substrate support surface. The patent document points out that factors such as internal stress of the wafer, support surface state and flatness may cause alignment deviation during bonding. This is obviously related to ASML's long-term research on wafer deformation compensation, position measurement and precision motion control technologies.
Of course, patent layout does not mean that mass-produced equipment is already mature. ASML has not yet publicly confirmed the commercial delivery time, customer certification progress or mass production performance of its hybrid bonding equipment. But this potential competition has begun to affect the market's expectations for traditional equipment enterprises. On October 6, Bank of America downgraded Besi's investment rating, which mentioned the competitive risk that ASML may enter the hybrid bonding market in the future.
For Besi, this risk is worthy of attention. In the traditional advanced packaging equipment market, Besi's important advantages come from long-term accumulation in precision mounting, assembly processes and hybrid bonding technology. Once ASML officially enters, it may form a new competitive force with its experience in nanoscale positioning, precision measurement and large-scale complex equipment system engineering.
However, from having key technical capabilities to developing competitive commercial equipment and then passing the mass production certification of wafer fabs, there is still a considerable long process of technology and commercialization.
Whether ASML can really challenge Besi ultimately depends on the alignment accuracy, throughput, yield, equipment stability, cost and customer certification progress of the equipment, and cannot be judged solely based on patents or supply chain news.
Why Has Hybrid Bonding Become the Focus of Competition? 
An important background for front-end equipment giants to enter advanced packaging one after another is that chip interconnection technology is changing.
In traditional 2.5D and 3D packaging, chips usually establish electrical connections through Micro-bumps. Thermal Compression Bonding (TCB) achieves reliable connection between solder and metal pads by applying temperature and pressure. This process is widely used in the field of high-performance computing and memory chips, but with the increase of chip stacking layers and the improvement of interconnection density, traditional micro-bump structures are gradually facing higher requirements in terms of pitch, connection height, parasitic effect and thermomechanical reliability.
Hybrid bonding provides another technical route. It combines direct dielectric bonding with metal interconnection to reduce the dependence on traditional solder bumps, thus making it possible to achieve smaller interconnection pitch, higher connection density and more compact chip stacking structure.
In May 2026, Imec, the Belgian microelectronics research center, and EV Group announced that they had achieved a 200nm copper interconnection pitch in wafer-to-wafer hybrid bonding research. The research team achieved a post-bond copper pad overlay deviation of less than 40nm for all test chips on 300mm wafers.
Transmission electron microscope image of the daisy chain structure on a 200nm hexagonal pad grid with hybrid pads of the same size and 25% designed copper density. (Image source: imec/IEEE)

Applied Materials opens $5B semiconductor innovation center
The EPIC Center is the world’s largest semiconductor equipment and process technology research and development facility, the company said.

A render of Applied Materials' new Equipment and Process Innovation and Commercialization Center. The company announced the center, where capital investment is expected to reach $5 billion, at its Sunnyvale, California, campus on Oct. 12.
Courtesy of Applied Materials
Listen to the article
3 min 
This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback .
Dive Brief:
Applied Materials , an equipment, services and software supplier for chipmakers, has opened its multibillion-dollar Equipment and Process Innovation and Commercialization Center to collaborate with industry on next-generation technologies.
Leading chipmakers, systems companies, equipment partners and research universities will work at the center to develop advanced chipmaking processes, as well as to move technologies from early-stage research to high-volume manufacturing faster, Applied Materials said.
The 600,000-square-foot facility is located at the company’s campus in Sunnyvale, California, and has near four acres of advanced cleanroom space. Applied Materials said it expects capital spending to reach $5 billion as new customer projects begin.
Dive Insight:
The news comes several months after Applied Materials announced it had partnered with South Korea-based SK Hynix to accelerate memory innovation and address semiconductor-related challenges at the EPIC Center. The agreement was reached as technology firms navigate a global shortage of memory chips driven by surging artificial intelligence demand.
According to Applied Materials, the EPIC Center will “reinvent” the standard research and development model in the semiconductor industry. The standard model typically involves handing off foundational materials research, equipment and process development, and process integration and pilot produciton from one siloed environment to the next.
“The EPIC Center is designed to remove these handoffs, putting the people who invent the materials, build the equipment, and make the chips together in a state-of-the-art facility purpose-built for commercialization,” the company said. “The technologies the AI era demands are too complex and too consequential for any one company to invent alone.”
Applied Materials said it expects the center’s operating model to provide chipmakers early access to advanced materials and equipment, shorter learning cycles and a faster path to volume production. 
Materials innovation has “outgrown serial development” and “demands coordinated development and integrated solutions,” Prabu Raja, president of Applied Materials’ semiconductor products group, said in a statement. “EPIC is the only place where materials, process technology and equipment will be innovated in parallel, which increases the success rate of new materials and technologies.”
Partners in the EPIC Center “span the AI technology stack” and include TSMC, Intel, SK Hynix, Micron, Samsung Electronics, Broadcom and Advantest, along with Arizona State University, Stanford University, University of California, Berkeley and other institutions. More companies and organizations are expected to join the center over time.
Applied Materials reported $7.01 billion in Q1 revenue , above the midpoint of its guided range, citing increased demand for leading-edge logic, high-bandwidth memory and advanced packaging.

What We Thought of ASML Holding’s Earnings
Last quarter, ASML Holding ASML announced plans to expand low-NA EUV and immersion DUV capacity by 30% in 2027 and another 30% in 2028. These plans seem already outdated, as management has acknowledged this might not be enough to meet customer demand.
Why it matters: ASML’s backlog keeps growing, with 2027 fully booked and significant order intake already for 2028. In our view, the most important disclosure from these earnings was that ASML is having first conversations with customers for 2029 and 2030 orders. DRAM makers seem the most open to talking about 2029-30 already.
While we still see some upside to our 2028 revenue and EPS forecast as ASML tries to expand capacity beyond 30% with its existing footprint, we believe most of it is already priced in. What could push the stock higher is order visibility that confirms 2029 and 2030 as “growth years.”
The bottom line: We maintain our wide Morningstar Economic Moat Rating and EUR 1,800 fair value estimate.
After 28% sales growth in both 2027 and 2028, reaching EUR 56 and EUR 71.5 billion respectively, we model a return to low-double-digit growth in 2029 and 2030, with sales reaching EUR 88 billion in 2030. Should management confirm the first 2029 orders over the next six months, our 2029-30 forecast would gain credibility, and the stock price could converge toward our fair value estimate.
Our bull case would require 2029 to book as quickly and as fully as 2028 has. If customers place orders at a fast pace in the coming months, sales growth in 2029-30 could exceed our low-double-digit forecast.
Key stats: Beyond expanding capacity, ASML continues to aggressively develop upgrades to low-NA EUV and immersion DUV output. Installed base management revenue reached EUR 3.3 billion, EUR 400 million higher than expected, thanks to the upgrade business, as customers look to extract more productivity from their machines. Upgrades were the main driver of the 57.5% gross margin this quarter, above guidance of 55.0%-57.0%.

Published Wed, Oct 14 2026 1:14 AM EDT Updated Wed, Oct 14 2026 4:45 AM EDT 
Arjun Kharpal @/in/arjunkharpal/ @ArjunKharpal 
WATCH LIVE 
Key Points
ASML said some customers are "expressing an interest" in placing orders with the company in 2029 and 2030, providing investors with a view into longer-term demand.
The Dutch chip giant said it is looking at ways to increase capacity for 2028 beyond the 30% increase it had previously forecast as demand remains strong.
The company also raised the lower end of its sales forecast for 2026.
In this article
ASML 
TSM 
Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT 
ASML said Wednesday that some of its customers are expressing interest in placing orders for its critical semiconductor tools for 2029 and 2030 as the company reported third-quarter profit that beat expectations.
The comments will likely comfort investors who have been looking to assess the longer-term demand outlook for ASML's lithography machines.
"Our customers continue to increase their short- and medium-term equipment demand forecasts with us, driven primarily by their views on the size and duration of AI-related investments," CEO Christophe Fouquet said in a press release. 
"In light of their demand visibility, some customers are expressing an interest in placing orders with us for 2029 and even 2030."
ASML is the only company in the world that produces extreme ultraviolet lithography machines, a key tool used by the likes of TSMC to make the world's most advanced semiconductors. 
Investors closely watch the Dutch company's earnings for signs of AI-related chip demand. 
watch now 
VIDEO 3:47 03:47 
ASML races to expand capacity on strong AI-driven demand
Squawk Box Europe 
Fouquet said current supply planned for 2027 and 2028 will not fully meet the demand of its customers. The company is "investigating ways" to increase capacity for 2028 beyond the 30% increase it had previously forecast. 
ASML has now updated its guidance three times this year, upping its full-year forecast for the second time in July, and on Wednesday it raised the lower end of its sales forecast for 2026. 
The company now expects net sales of between 44 billion euros and 45 billion euros ($49.3 billion to $50.4 billion). The previous lower end of the forecast was for 43 billion euros.
ASML also said it expects fourth-quarter net sales of between 14.2 billion euros and 15.2 billion euros. The upper end of the range is ahead of LSEG consensus estimates of 14.2 billion euros. 
ASML's stock was around 2% higher in early trade in Europe. Shares of the company have rallied 56% this year. 
ASML shares year-to-date
During the quarter, Samsung and TSMC, the world's two biggest chipmakers, committed to using ASML's High NA extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines. High NA EUV is ASML's next-generation tool, which analysts see as key to the Dutch firm's future growth.
For the third quarter, here's how ASML did versus LSEG consensus estimates:
Net sales: 11.66 billion euros versus 11.72 billion euros expected
Net profit: 4.96 billion euros versus 4.1 billion euros expected 
ASML sticks to China forecast 
The semiconductor equipment maker said it expects China sales to account for 20% of its total business, sticking to a prior forecast.
While ASML holds an effective monopoly on EUV machines, a July report from The Information suggested an unnamed Chinese company had begun manufacturing an immersion deep ultraviolet lithography (DUV) machine, citing people familiar with the matter.
ASML dominates the manufacturing of DUV machines, which are less advanced than EUV. China has been ramping up its domestic semiconductor supply chain, with some investors concerned it could challenge the European and U.S. dominance. However, analysts raised questions about China's ability to ramp up its own DUV technology. 
ASML meanwhile has faced challenges in China over the last few years. The company is restricted from selling EUV and some DUV tools to China.

Mkango Magnetic Materials Ltd. (AIM/TSX-V: MKA) said HyProMag USA has secured power capacity with Oncor Electric Delivery Company for its planned Texas rare earth magnet recycling and manufacturing hub.
The power allocation covers the initial cutting and finishing operation and the proposed Phase 1 development , with a pathway to additional capacity for Phase 2 through a substation upgrade.
HyProMag USA expects the electricity supplied to the facility to come predominantly from renewable energy sources .
PegasusTSI has started a contractor-selection process for the cutting and finishing facility, while Weston Solutions is progressing permitting activities.
The first stage is targeted for commissioning during the first half of 2027 .
That operation will not initially manufacture magnet blocks from recycled material in Texas. Instead, it is designed to cut, finish and qualify NdFeB magnet blocks supplied from other HyProMag Group operations .
The facility is intended to establish US finishing capability, customer qualification processes and workforce training ahead of the larger integrated development.
HyProMag USA plans to operate to recognised magnetic-material and quality standards, including ASTM A977/A977M and systems aligned with ISO 9001.
The larger Phase 1 Texas Hub is targeted for completion in mid-2028 . It is designed to produce approximately 550 tonnes per annum of sintered NdFeB magnet blocks and finished magnets , together with around 484 tonnes of co-products, giving approximately 1,034 tonnes per annum of total payable production .
A subsequent Phase 2 expansion envisages approximately 1,048 tonnes per annum of NdFeB magnet blocks and cylinders plus 478 tonnes of co-products, taking total payable production to approximately 1,526 tonnes per annum .
Importantly, those figures are design capacities rather than current production or confirmed future output .
CoTec chief executive Julian Treger said securing power, advancing permitting and commencing contractor selection further de-risk the project and support the goal of establishing a domestic US rare earth magnet supply chain.
For investors, the significance is that the Texas Hub is moving from engineering and planning towards site infrastructure, permitting and contractor procurement .
The next tangible milestones are the award of construction contracts, permitting progress and successful commissioning of the initial cutting and finishing operation in H1 2027 , followed by execution of the larger integrated Phase 1 development targeted for 2028.

CoTec Holdings Corp. Notes HyproMag USA Secures Power and Advances Project Readiness for Texas Rare Earth Magnet Recycling and Manufacturing Hub
Investing News Network 
October 13, 2026 
VANCOUVER, BC / ACCESS Newswire / October 13, 2026 / CoTec Holdings Corp. ( TSXV:CTH )(OTCQX:CTHCF) ("CoTec" or the "Company") notes the press release issued today by its joint venture, HyProMag USA, LLC ("HyProMag USA"), providing an update on development activities for its Texas Hub rare earth magnet recycling and manufacturing project in Dallas-Fort Worth, Texas (the "Texas Hub"). Following the commencement of formal power supply discussions announced on June 22, 2026, i HyProMag USA has secured electrical power capacity with Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC ("Oncor") for the Texas Hub development and expects the facility's electricity requirements to be supplied predominantly from renewable energy resources.
Key Highlights 
Power capacity secured: Power capacity secured with Oncor for both cutting and finishing operations and the Phase 1 development, with a pathway through a sub-station upgrade to provide power for Phase 2.
Contractor selection and permitting underway: Pegasus TSI, Inc. ("Pegasus") has commenced contractor selection for cutting and finishing operations and Weston Solutions, Inc. ("Weston") is advancing permitting activities.
Cutting and finishing operations targeted for H1 2027: Targeted commissioning of cutting and finishing operations in H1 2027 with the processing of neodymium iron boron ("NdFeB") magnet blocks, initially supplied from HyProMag Group operations, to produce finished magnets.
Phase 1 development: Phase 1 development is targeted for completion in mid-2028 and is designed to produce approximately 550 tonnes per annum ("tpa") of NdFeB magnet blocks and finished magnets and approximately 484 tpa of co-products, representing approximately 1,034 tpa of total payable production.
Phase 2 development: Phase 2 development envisions expansion to approximately 1,526 tpa of total payable production.
Renewable energy supply: Electricity supply expected to be sourced predominantly from renewable energy resources.
Julian Treger, Chief Executive Officer of CoTec Holdings Corp. , commented: "Securing power with Oncor, advancing permitting activities through Weston Solutions and commencing contractor selection are important milestones for the Texas Hub. Initial cutting and finishing operations in 2027 are expected to establish U.S. magnet finishing and qualification capabilities aligned with internationally recognized magnetic material and quality standards, while the full Phase 1 development will deliver integrated recycling and magnet manufacturing capacity. Together, these activities further de-risk the project and demonstrate continued progress towards establishing a domestic and sustainable rare earth magnet supply chain in the United States." 
Cutting and Finishing Operations 
Cutting and finishing operations in 2027 comprise the initial magnet finishing and qualification facility, enabling production and qualification of finished NdFeB magnets using magnet blocks supplied from HyProMag Group operations. The facility is designed to process NdFeB magnet blocks and support qualification of finished magnets in accordance with ASTM A977/A977M, the national classification standard for magnetic materials, together with quality management systems aligned with ISO 9001 and customer-specific quality, performance and traceability requirements. The objective is to establish qualification capabilities that meet the requirements of U.S. customers and establish a strategic training facility for the finishing of NdFeB magnets in advance of the main Texas Hub developments.
Permitting and Contractor Selection 
Weston is advancing permitting activities for the Texas Hub, while HyProMag USA's engineering partner Pegasus has commenced a Request for Quotation ("RFQ") process for the selection of a general contractor for cutting and finishing operations. Pegasus and BBA USA Inc. are HyProMag USA's U.S.-based engineering, procurement and construction management firms.
Phase 1 and Phase 2 Development 
Phase 1 represents the first integrated recycling and magnet manufacturing stage of the Texas Hub and is designed to produce approximately 550 tpa of sintered NdFeB magnet blocks and finished magnets, together with approximately 484 tpa of co-products, representing total payable production of approximately 1,034 tpa. Upon completion of Phase 2, the Texas Hub is expected to produce approximately 1,048 tpa of sintered NdFeB magnet blocks and cylinders, together with approximately 478 tpa of co-products, representing total payable production of approximately 1,526 tpa.
About HyProMag USA 
HyProMag USA is developing advanced rare earth magnet recycling and manufacturing operations to establish a secure domestic U.S. supply chain for NdFeB magnets, essential components for AI infrastructure, defense systems, robotics, electric vehicles, and advanced electronics. Leveraging the revolutionary Hydrogen Processing of Magnet Scrap ("HPMS") technology, developed over 15 years with over US$100 million in R&D investment, HyProMag USA delivers faster magnet-to-magnet short-loop recycling that uses 88% less energy and reduces carbon emissions by 85% compared to conventional methods. HPMS accepts a wide range of magnet-bearing feedstocks - including end-of-life EV motors, data-center and industrial equipment, consumer electronics, and manufacturing scrap - enabling recovery of magnet-grade material without chemical processing.
Ownership 
HyProMag USA LLC is owned 50:50 by CoTec and HyProMag Limited. HyProMag Limited is 100% owned by Maginito Limited, which is owned 79.4% by Mkango Magnetic Materials Limited (AIM/TSX-V: MKA) and 20.6% by CoTec.

Air Liquide to build new Air Separation Unit at its Fairfield facility in New South Wales
PR Newswire 
October 7, 2026 2 min read 
AI.PA 
+1.98% 
MELBOURNE, Australia, Oct. 8, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Air Liquide announces a new investment to build and operate a new Air Separation Unit (ASU) and its related infrastructure at its existing Fairfield Facility located in Yennora, New South Wales - Australia. This will enhance local supply chain reliability for industrial and medical gases across Australia. 
Air Liquide to build new Air Separation Unit in New South Wales The new ASU will produce nitrogen and oxygen, critical gases to support the daily operations and long-term growth of key Australian sectors , including food and beverage processing, healthcare and medical facilities, mining and advanced manufacturing. 
The ASU is expected to start-up in 2028. 
Tim Kehoe, Managing Director of Air Liquide Pacific said: "Expanding our air gas capacity demonstrates Air Liquide's long-term commitment to fueling the growth of Australian industries with essential gases they depend on every day. With the new ASU in New South Wales, we are reinforcing our commitment to serving our customers and enhancing our supply chain resilience." 
Air Liquide Australia 
Air Liquide Australia started its operations in 1957 and currently employs 400+ employees across Pacific. In Australia, Air Liquide operates air separation plants, CO₂ plants and gas filling facilities. Air Liquide provides innovative and customer-focused solutions and services and supports the Australian economy through a unique blend of advanced equipment, processes & systems, supported by a highly engaged and competent workforce. 
Air Liquide is a leader in gases, technologies, and services for numerous economic sectors. As an invisible yet essential cornerstone of industry and healthcare for more than a century, the Group's molecules pave the way for progress by delivering useful and innovative solutions to customers, patients, and society. 
Present in 59 countries with approximately 65,000 employees, the Group serves 4.3 million customers and patients. With revenues close to 27 billion euros in 2025 and solid foundations, Air Liquide combines performance with lasting value creation for all its stakeholders. With "Beyond", its strategic plan through 2030, the Group has set an ambitious roadmap to accelerate its profitable growth trajectory and continue inventing the future. 
Air Liquide is listed on the Euronext Paris stock exchange (compartment A) and is a member of the CAC 40, CAC 40 ESG, EURO STOXX 50, FTSE4Good, and Dow Jones Best-in-Class Europe indexes.

CPHI 2026: Big Thermo Fisher announcements include new manufacturing lines in US and Italy 
As the firm continues to expand its global footprint, we spoke with an executive about what life science companies should consider when choosing research and manufacturing partners.
Josh Abbott , News Editor, BioProcess International October 7, 2026
schedule 3 Min Read 
stock.adobe.com 
link 
Biotech giant Thermo Fisher Scientific made a splash this week at CPHI Milan 2026 with a number of big announcements spanning multiple service areas. The company is expanding its sterile drug product lines in Plainville, Massachusetts, and at its sites in Monza and Ferentino, Italy. 
The expansions will support the development and commercial manufacturing of vials and prefilled syringes. According to the firm, the Plainville expansion includes the introduction of bioprocessing equipment to the site, expanding US-based GMP monoclonal antibody (mAb) manufacturing capacity. 
Thermo Fisher is also expanding its clinical supply storage with a 52,000-square-foot expansion in Bohemia, New York, that will increase clinical label manufacturing capacity. The company is additionally growing its footprint in Japan – doubling that country’s clinical supply storage, distribution, and secondary packaging capacity – with a new facility in Tokyo. 
Related: Revisiting build or buy: What a year of scale-up changed for radiopharmaceutical programs 
“Drug development increasingly depends on decisions and capabilities that span traditional boundaries, from development and manufacturing to clinical supply and clinical execution,” said Mike Shafer, EVP and president of Biopharma Services at Thermo Fisher Scientific. “We’re investing not only in capacity, but in how those capabilities connect. That gives our customers greater continuity as they navigate critical transitions, scale their programs, and prepare for commercialization.” 
These moves, in addition to announcements the company made in the small-molecule space, further cement Thermo Fisher’s standing as a global pharma service provider. BioProcess International spoke with Anil Kane, executive director and global head of technical & scientific affairs at Thermo Fisher, about the challenges and advantages of partnering with a company that operates under an integrated model, offering both contract development and manufacturing organization (CDMO) and contract research organization (CRO) services. 
“Companies have traditionally selected partners function by function: a CRO for clinical development, a CDMO for manufacturing, another provider for clinical supply,” Kane told us. “Moving away from it requires rethinking how a development program is managed, not just changing vendors.” 
He said that developers might choose to work with multiple specialized service providers to maintain flexibility and retain access to specialized expertise in each area. The trade-off comes in separating elements that are interdependent. 
“A manufacturing decision can affect clinical supply, an analytical issue can push out downstream timelines, and a shift in enrollment assumptions can throw off inventory and manufacturing plans,” he said. “When those activities are managed separately, it can be difficult to see the downstream impact of a decision until it has already caused a delay.” 
Related: Responsible outsourcing: Avoiding common pitfalls in biopharma partnerships 
Nevertheless, he acknowledged that every situation is different. For programs that are already underway, transitioning to an integrated model can create further challenges. 
“If a company is already well into a program, changing partners or governance structures all at once can create unnecessary disruption,” he said. “In those situations, it can make sense to look for natural inflection points in development where greater integration can be introduced without putting the program at risk.” 
For some companies, such an inflection point may be found between phases. Thermo Fisher commissioned a study by the Tufts Center for the Study of Drug Development (CSDD), which Kane cited as illustrating greater financial return for integrated programs in Phase III than in Phase I for both mAb and small-molecule programs. 
But Kane once again stressed that the decision will not be the same for every company in every situation. “Development phase is only part of the equation,” he said. “Integration can also be valuable earlier in development when the science is complex, timelines are compressed, manufacturing and clinical strategies need to evolve together, or a smaller biotech has limited internal resources to coordinate multiple partners.”

content_text:
Bayer’s CEO cut manager ranks by 70%. Now comes the hard part
By Diane Brady 
Diane Brady 
Executive Editorial Director 
By Diane Brady 
Diane Brady 
Executive Editorial Director 
October 7, 2026, 5:02 AM ET 
Bayer AG CEO Bill Anderson during the Federation of German Industries (BDI) Day of Industry conference in Berlin on June 22, 2026. Krisztian Bocsi/Bloomberg via Getty Images 
Add Fortune on Google for similar content.
Add us on Google 
Add us on Google 
In today’s CEO Daily: What happens after you flatten your company? 
The big leadership story: Why Oura really pulled its IPO
The markets: Mostly down after the S&P 500 closed at a record high on Tuesday.
Plus: All the news and watercooler chat from Fortune .
Good morning . After you’ve streamlined and transformed and flattened your company, how do you get it to grow again? I recently asked that question to Bayer CEO Bill Anderson, who’s done all of the above at the 163-year-old health science giant. He’s reduced the number of managers from about 16,000 to 4,500 (in a company of 88,000) and replaced hierarchy and annual budgets with 5,000 small teams working on 90-day cycles. So what’s next?
Recommended Video 
“Our ambition, for the last three years, basically, was to survive,” he told me, as we sipped takeout coffee in an empty corner of New York’s Javits Center last month. “How much are we willing to stretch ourselves now and put out a bold ambition for what this company can be and fight for that?”
Good question. Bayer announced plans to invest $2.2 billion in a new Ohio manufacturing site last week. Global COO Sebastian Guth recently wrote in Fortune that the company stopped assigning sales targets. Investors are newly enthusiastic as Bayer’s stock is up 57% over the past year (versus about 21% for BASF and 14% for Novartis) but flat over the past three years (versus 43% and 47% growth, respectively). Anderson has improved profitability and won a Supreme Court ruling that addresses liability claims predating his arrival, but the real test will be whether he can continue to drive revenue and profit growth .
.contents]:contents flex items-center"> 
Anderson has found that giving people more authority doesn’t necessarily increase their willingness to make tough decisions. “We have a nice culture” that’s “a little softer” on things like “courageous authenticity and decisiveness.”
To address that, he started at the top: “The job of the leaders is not to manage people, and it’s not to decide the goals, and then, you know, cascade them. No, forget that. The job of the leaders is to set the vision. That’s very different than telling everyone what to do,” he said. “We are putting 95% of decision making at the bottom, not delegating it down in the hierarchy.” He ranks his priorities in descending order: Mission first, employees second, shareholders third, senior management last. 
What’s oddly heartening is the realization that Anderson doesn’t have all the answers. It shows that transformation is ongoing and hard. “This is not a culture program or a communication program,” said Anderson. “Ninety-nine percent of all corporate transformations are not transformations. They’re just shuffling the boxes around.”

Top leadership news
Why Oura really pulled its IPO 
Oura blamed "uncertainty in the IPO market" for scrapping its offering hours before pricing, but experts suspect other causes : a steep $40-$44 per share price for a hardware-heavy company, the fact that only 27% of shares would be newly issued by the company, and the threat of an Apple ring. Oura says it has the “luxury of choosing our moment” to go public. 
.contents]:contents flex items-center" data-empty-mobile="true"> 
McDonald’s looks beyond meal deals 
.contents]:contents flex items-center" data-empty-desktop="true"> 
Discounts haven’t reversed slowing U.S. growth for McDonald’s. Rising beef costs and a crowded schedule of menu launches have added pressure on restaurants. CEO Chris Kempczinski is now offering franchisees $8.5 billion in support over 10 years as he pushes for restaurant upgrades and better service. 
Why Mikel Arteta had his DNA mapped 
Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta had his genome sequenced to better understand his health risks, prompting changes to his diet and sleep routines. He explains why looking after his own health is part of leading his team—and why he decided to talk about it publicly.

Japan’s Nikkei 225 was down 0.92%. South Korea’s KOSPI was down 1.98%. China’s markets are closed. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng was down 0.62%. India’s NIFTY 50 is down 0.84%. Bitcoin is down at $84k.

content_text:
Renishaw Expands Miskin Site as Demand Drives Manufacturing Growth 
October 7, 2026 
This year, engineering technologies business, Renishaw, is celebrating the 15th anniversary of the purchase of its Miskin site in South Wales, and the completion of the first phase of a further £70 million development of the facility. Announced in 2022, this is the largest capital investment project in the company’s history, which will ultimately double the size of the Miskin site, giving the company space to expand manufacturing capacity to meet rising demand for its world-leading precision metrology, additive manufacturing and position measurement products.
Renishaw has been committed to the manufacturing of its own products since its formation and uses many of these products within its machining facilities. Whilst much of its production is performed in the UK, at its Miskin, Stonehouse and Woodchester sites, it has carriedout the assembly of metrology products in Ireland since 1981, and also has a significant operation in Pune, India.
Renishaw completed the acquisition of the 193-acre site, situated to the west of Cardiff, from RobertBosch Ltd in September 2011. It started modest operations in May 2012 with a single production shift, having refurbished around 15% of the 416,000 sq ft (38,675 sqm) total building space, which primarily consisted of two large production halls. By the time of the formal opening of the facility in October 2012 by then First Minister of Wales, employee numbers were around 25, compared to around 950 today. Following the completion of the first development phase (Hall 3), usablespace has grown to 617,000 sq ft (57,350 sqm) and will total 880,000 sq ft (81,765 sqm) once Hall 4 is completed and operational, establishing the Miskin facility as one of the UK’s largest advanced manufacturing sites.
Renishaw has continued to invest throughout its tenure, with around £150 million spent to date on acquiring the site, refurbishing legacy buildings, developing the new halls, and installing advanced manufacturing equipment. The latter currently includes 134 CNC machine tools producing around one million parts per month, three PCB assembly lines, robotic assembly and automated warehousing, with more equipment on order to support customer requirements.
Manufacturing Capacity to Support Future Growth 
The latest phase of development demonstrates Renishaw’s long-term confidence in the UK and its commitment to creating highly skilled jobs and supporting economic growth for years to come.
Hall 3 is used to manufacture Renishaw’s metal additive manufacturing (AM) systems, AGILITY coordinate measuring machines (CMMs) and also houses a multimillion-pound automated storage andretrieval warehousing system. The company is currently experiencing strong demand for its AM systems, notably from the aerospace and defence (A&D) sector, and is also seeing growing demand for its high precision multi-sensor CMMs used to inspect complex components, including applications in the energy and Aerospace & Defence sectors.
Hall 4 was constructed as a shell building, with its future utilisation dependent on sales demand and capacity requirements. Due to exceptional demand for Renishaw’s position encoders from manufacturers of semiconductor equipment,driven by the growing adoption of artificial intelligence (AI), some of that additional capacity is now required, and Hall 4 will be partially occupied over the coming months. To support customers in this important sector, the company is also increasing its capital expenditure on equipment, especially new machine tools, electronics production and automated assembly.
Steve Oakes, Director of Position Measurement, said, “ Our encoders are used at all stages of the semiconductor production process, from manufacturing silicon wafers to packaging and testing individual devices. The semiconductor sector is highly cyclical, and we are currently seeing a ‘super cycle’, which is driving very high levels of investment across the entire supply chain. ”
A Focus on Sustainability 
Beyond increasing manufacturing capacity, the development of the new halls has been designed to deliver long-term operational and environmental benefits, supporting Renishaw’s wider commitment to achieving Net Zero greenhouse gas emissions across Scopes 1 and 2 by 2028. The company’s long term ambition is for all buildings at the Miskin site to operate at Net Zero, and both new halls have been designed to achieve Net Zero Carbon in Operation.
The high-performance buildings require significantly less energy than conventional industrial facilities, reducing operating costs and carbon emissions from the outset. Enhanced insulation in the walls, roofs and floors delivers thermal performance well beyond current building regulation requirements, while high-performance glazing minimises heat loss and reduces the energy required to maintain comfortable indoor conditions throughout the year.
Heating and cooling are provided by highly efficient electric heat pump systems, which generate multiple units of heating or cooling energy for every unit of electricity consumed. The system delivers approximately four units of heat and six units of cooling per unit of electricity, making it substantially more energy efficient and lower in carbon emissions than conventional gas-fired systems.
A key feature of the Miskin expansion is its extensive use of on-site renewable energy generation, delivering an estimated 200 MWh of clean electricity each year. Where additional electricity is required, renewable energy tariffs are used to further reduce the site’s carbon footprint.
The Miskin expansion has provided valuable opportunities to develop the skills of Renishaw’s apprentices and graduate engineers who have played an active role throughout the project. They have gained first-hand experience of delivering a major industrial development, and project engineering apprentices were embedded within the design teams responsible for the new development, contributing to layout planning, coordinating with multiple business functions, attending regular site visits and supporting the design of office and workshop facilities.
Commitment to The Future 
The expansion of the Miskin site represents a major long-term investment in UK manufacturing, sustainability and skills development. It reinforces Renishaw’s commitment to South Wales and the UK while providing a modern, low-carbon manufacturing environment that showcases the best of British engineering. As the site continues to evolve, the new facilities will play a vital role in supporting innovation, reducing carbon emissions and creating high-quality employment opportunities for years to come.
Jim Long, Director of Group Manufacturing, said, “ The strong growth we are currently seeing has highlighted the importance of in-house manufacturing and the control it gives us in meeting our quality, cost and delivery targets. This commitment to manufacturing is exemplified by the investment that we have made in Miskin over the past 15 years and I would like to thank the many people from across our business who have supported the development of this world-class facility.” 
He continued, “ A key aim of our facilities is to create an attractive and enjoyable working environment that inspires employees while creating a world-class environment that impresses visitors and presents a positive image of manufacturing.” 
Long concluded, “ The significant ongoing investment by our Board to increase our production capabilities demonstrates a huge vote of confidence in our manufacturing operations and people, at an exciting time for the business.” 
For more information: www.renishaw.com

content_text:
Sumitomo Chemical Signs India Semiconductor MoU
Sumitomo Chemical has signed a memorandum of understanding with Tata Electronics to explore a collaboration on building a semiconductor supply chain in India.
© J_News_photo - stock.adobe.com
Under the MoU, Sumitomo Chemical will examine measures for a stable supply of semiconductor materials, including the potential establishment of a semiconductor chemicals facility in India. 
India's government has made growing its semiconductor industry a national strategic priority, and Tata Electronics is building the country's first front-end semiconductor fabrication plant. With India's semiconductor and materials markets set to expand, Sumitomo Chemical sees the project as a way to strengthen the industry's foundation locally. 
Sumitomo Chemical has made semiconductor materials a priority within its ICT & Mobility Solutions sector, supplying advanced photoresists and semiconductor chemicals, and building a reputation in high-purity chemicals through ultra-high-purity technologies, quality assurance and global supply capabilities. 
The company has also been expanding this business globally, growing capacity in Japan and South Korea, opening a site in Texas in 2022, and acquiring Asia Union Electronic Chemical Corporation in 2026, with plants in Taiwan and Nevada. It has also launched Advanced High-Purity Chemical Centers in Japan and South Korea in 2026 to develop production and recycling technologies. The potential Tata Electronics partnership will help it assess further opportunities in India.

Oct 5, 2026

Highlights 
Proterial plans a ₹2,250-crore, 1,200-tonne/year sintered NdFeB magnet plant in Andhra Pradesh and is among 20 bidders for India's ₹7,280-crore rare-earth permanent-magnet scheme.
The company's heavy-rare-earth-free magnets eliminate dysprosium and terbium but still rely on neodymium, making the technology rare-earth-risk reduction, not elimination.
Proterial's FEV motor concept combining amorphous-alloy cores with HRE-free magnets simulates 300 kW output, 27% weight reduction, and 97.9% WLTP efficiency.
India's subsidy program targets the full oxide-to-magnet chain, recognizing that local sintering alone does not resolve upstream NdPr feedstock dependence.
Proterial's new Motor Solutions Department signals a strategic shift from component supply toward full motor-system optimization for xEV applications.

Air Liquide launches first ever €4 billion buyback under new 2030 strategy
Vahid Karaahmetovic 
October 5, 2026 2 min read 
AI.PA 
+1.98% 
AIRP 
Investing.com -- Air Liquide unveiled a new strategic plan through 2030 on Monday, targeting annual growth in recurring net earnings per share (EPS) of about 10% and launching its first-ever share buyback program, worth €4 billion over 2027-2028. 
Before you buy NVIDIA: our AI model's stock picks are beating the market by 120%+. See the list now » 
The plan, named "BEYOND," aims for compound annual growth of 10%, plus or minus 2 percentage points, in recurring net EPS from the end of 2025 to the end of 2030. The French industrial gases group also targets recurring return on capital employed (ROCE) above 11% in 2030, even as it significantly raises industrial investment. 
To get there, Air Liquide said it is leaning on three levers. It expects sales to grow at a compound annual rate of 5%, plus or minus 1 point, outpacing industrial production by a factor of two to three. It also targets a cumulative operating margin improvement of 400 to 600 basis points over 2026-2030. 
The third lever is capital allocation of more than €40 billion over the period, covering investments, acquisitions, dividends and buybacks. More than half will go toward industrial investments and acquisitions, with industrial investment decisions of about €24 billion planned, Air Liquide said. The buyback will be paired with continued dividend growth, it noted. 
Not finding the right stocks? Our AI's list of investor-grade stock picks for October just dropped » 
Air Liquide identified four priority markets: electronics and artificial intelligence, energy transition, healthcare and space. The company expects electronics sales to grow at a weighted average annual rate above 10% over 2026-2030, citing demand from larger chip fabrication projects and government policies encouraging local fab development. 
"With BEYOND, Air Liquide opens an ambitious new strategic chapter in its profitable growth trajectory. The Group enters this cycle on solid foundations and with committed teams serving our customers and patients," said CEO François Jackow. "In a constantly evolving environment, powered by the success of our ADVANCE plan, the resilience of our business model, our innovation capabilities, and our leading market positions, our roadmap is clear: reach a new frontier in lasting value creation." 
He said the group's profitability now allows it to go beyond reinvestment, including through the buyback and annual employee share purchase plans. 
The company also reaffirmed environmental targets, including a 33% cut in Scope 1 and 2 carbon dioxide emissions by 2035 from 2020 levels and carbon neutrality by 2050.
